intent: Mark up a key cap or short label so it reads as a key on screen.
typical_uses: A single key named in running help text or a menu item (Esc closes the dialog)
One key of a chorded shortcut, grouped by KbdGroup (Ctrl, K)

dont_use_when.situation: An interactive control that happens to look like a key
A command line or other text the user types verbatim

instead.target: the consuming application's own code or monospace text styling
instead.note: This kit ships no code text component, and no kit component is a substitute for one: Kbd marks key caps and short chords, not typed-out command lines.

mounted_in.container: running text in the consuming application
mounted_in.note: A single key is named inline in a paragraph or a hint, with no kit container around it.

invariants.text: Kbd is display-only decoration: the kit's stylesheet renders it with `pointer-events: none` and `user-select: none`, so it never receives clicks, focus or selection, and it carries no ARIA role of its own - the semantics are the native kbd element's alone.

anti_patterns.dont: Attach the shortcut's click or key handler to the Kbd itself
anti_patterns.do_instead: Wire the handler on the real control (a Button, a menu item, a window keydown listener) and keep Kbd purely to name the key in text

good.title: A key cap named in running text
One key of a chord, grouped by KbdGroup

bad.title: Making the key cap itself clickable
bad.why: Kbd renders with `pointer-events: none` and carries no interaction of its own, so a handler on it never fires from a click on the glyph. Put the handler on a real control and keep Kbd for display.

bad.title: A variant prop guessed from another component
bad.why: Kbd takes no kit-specific props; every prop is the native kbd element's. There is no variant axis here - the look is fixed by the kit's stylesheet.
